CMU Miami is designed to move beyond the traditional hub-and-spoke model of university expansion. Rather than simply extending individual programs or research activities into a new city, CMU Miami will develop into a comprehensive university campus where education and research are equally central to the mission, built to the same standards of academic excellence that define CMU.
“We are deeply grateful to Ken Griffin for his extraordinary vision, partnership and belief in what Carnegie Mellon can achieve,” said
CMU President

Once complete, the state-of-the-art campus will support more than 3,500 undergraduate, master’s and PhD students, nearly 300 faculty and over 600 staff members. Construction is slated to begin in 2027. The current plan, pending regulatory approvals, sees the first students enrolling in 2028.
Located on more than 35 acres in Wynwood — in the heart of Miami — the campus will support a comprehensive student experience and an interdisciplinary environment designed for learning, research and collaboration. Plans include space for industry research labs and venture studios, creating opportunities for students, faculty, industry and community partners to work alongside one another. The campus itself will serve as a living laboratory for new ideas, while creating opportunities for collaboration across CMU’s locations.
"Every great Carnegie Mellon story begins with partnership," Jahanian said. "Our relationship with Pittsburgh has shaped CMU for more than a century, and we believe the connections we build in Miami will enrich both cities. We look forward to listening, learning and working alongside our neighbors to create new opportunities for collaboration, innovation and shared prosperity."

A university without borders, Carnegie Mellon extends its impact far beyond Pittsburgh through a global network of programs, partnerships and research initiatives spanning Europe, Africa, Asia and beyond, including campuses in Qatar and Rwanda. Carnegie Mellon’s faculty and alumni include dozens of Nobel Prize and Turing Award recipients, as well as members of prestigious academies and leaders across industry, government and the arts worldwide.

About Ken Griffin and Griffin Catalyst
Ken Griffin is the founder and CEO of Citadel and the founder of Citadel Securities and Griffin Catalyst, the civic engagement initiative that encompasses his philanthropic and community impact efforts.
Ken founded Citadel in 1990, and today, it is recognized as one of the world’s most successful hedge funds. The Citadel team has delivered extraordinary results for pension plans, university endowments, hospital systems, foundations, and research institutions that deliver meaningful impact for society, from curing cancer with immunotherapy to making scientific breakthroughs in particle physics.
In 2002, Ken and his partners established Citadel Securities, a leading global market maker. Today, it is one of the world’s largest liquidity providers, serving more than 1,600 institutional clients and millions of American families, and has proven transformative in enhancing competition in capital markets worldwide.
Ken is also a passionate philanthropist.

Department Vision, Mission and Values

Department Vision, Mission and Values

Vision

The Carnegie Mellon University Department of Athletics, Physical Education and Recreation will provide a transformative and inclusive educational experience that nurtures competitiveness, wellness, belonging and resilience, and provides students with a leadership framework to live healthy and impactful lives.

Mission

To educate students through sport as they compete and strive for comprehensive excellence.

To deliver an unparalleled student-athlete experience that serves to develop the next generation of thought leaders and innovators.

To achieve at an elite level and establish a championship Division III culture.

To teach balance and wellness through diverse recreational program offerings and opportunities.

To complement and enhance the learning that transpires in Carnegie Mellon’s classrooms.

To excel academically at a world-renowned institution and prepare students to impact the world in myriad ways.

To align resources — human, capital, financial — with the strategic priorities guiding a transformative student experience.

Values

Integrity,
reflected as a core component of everything we do.

Wellness,
reflected in the way we educate and prepare students for all facets of their lives.

SMART Program

SMART Program

The Sports Medicine Assessment of Risk Tendencies (SMART) Protocol is a proactive, cutting-edge approach to providing varsity student-athletes with services they need to remain healthy and educated about their well-being. The goal of the program is to prevent, recognize, refer and respond to any health-related issues that impact the varsity student-athlete population, and allow for better health and performance on and off the field of play.

The Sports Medicine Staff collaborates with members of Health Services, Counseling and Psychological Services (CaPS) and Student Life to provide a comprehensive and multi-disciplinary educational program for Carnegie Mellon University’s student-athlete population.  The educational sessions are made up of 4 topics: Nutrition, Drugs and Alcohol, Mental Health, and Sexual Assault. Speakers provide information about each topic and have open discussions to better engage the varsity student athletes. The SMART program provides information and tools for the varsity student athletes to make educated decisions when it comes to these areas.

Mission

The sports medicine team is committed to treating our varsity student-athletes with a holistic approach.

SMART Program

Mission

The sports medicine team is committed to treating our varsity student-athletes with a holistic approach.  We believe that we must treat the whole person; this is achieved by addressing mental and social factors, in addition to treating the physical symptoms of injuries.

Goal

The SMART program’s goal is to prevent, recognize, refer and respond to potential risk tendencies that varsity student-athletes may experience in a collegiate setting.  Topics included but not limited to disordered eating, substance abuse, mental wellness, sexual assault and dating violence prevention.

Team will consist of:

Coordinator of Student-Athlete Wellness Certified Athletic Trainers Team Physicians Director of Student Health Services Student Health Services Nutritionist | Health Promotion Specialist Director of CaPS Athletic Director Office of Community Standards and Integrity Office of Title IX Initiatives

| | "The SMART program helps to introduce teams to the resources available on campus. The seminars show us how we can deal with a wide range of issues from homework and class conflicts to drug and alcohol use, through Carnegie Mellon University’s services for athletes."

The Plaidvocates

The Plaidvocates

Mission

The Plaidvocates is a peer health and wellness advocacy program for student-athletes that supports the well-being of CMU’s varsity athletics community. This peer-to-peer volunteer organization is comprised of student-athletes that lead by adopting health-promoting behaviors, provide year-round support and mentorship, and empower their peers to engage in responsible and informed decision making.

The Plaidvocates are educated and trained throughout the year to be able to listen, promote and provide support and information on stress and time management, nutrition, alcohol, drug use and other health related topics. The Plaidvocates function as a resource and role model for their peers by providing one-on-one interaction, educational programming and leadership.

Having trouble juggling your academics and practice? Want some advice about healthy snacks during the day? Want to talk to someone about the class that’s stressing you out? Have questions about how to say no when asked to have a drink? Do you feel that it is time to reach out and talk to someone?

The Plaidvocates

Have questions about how to say no when asked to have a drink? Do you feel that it is time to reach out and talk to someone?

If you have questions, concerns or just need to talk to someone, a Plaidvocate is able to set up a time to meet with you and help.

Not sure which Plaidvocate to contact?

The Sports Medicine team can help you choose a Plaidvocate that is best suited to assist with your specific situation if you are having trouble deciding on a contact.  Please send an email to
cmu.atc@gmail.com
and they will forward your information to a Plaidvocate, who will in turn contact you.

When contacting a Plaidvocate, please email them your name and a general reason why you want to meet and talk with them.

To ensure the Plaidvocates are providing proper support, each peer-to-peer interaction will be discussed with a member of the CMU sports medicine staff. All names and team information will remain anonymous unless the individual is determined to be in imminent danger of hurting themselves or others.

Tartan Facts

Tartan Facts

Who founded Carnegie Mellon University?

Carnegie Technical Schools was founded in 1900 by Andrew Carnegie. Twelve years later it became known as the Carnegie Institute of Technology. In 1967, the school merged with Mellon Institute and became what is known today as Carnegie Mellon University.

What is a Tartan?

The Carnegie Mellon athletic teams are nicknamed the "Tartans" as a nod to Andrew Carnegie's Scottish heritage. A tartan is often misrepresented as a fierce warrior from either the Asian tundra or Scottish highlands. In actuality, a Tartan is a twilled woolen fabric with a plaid design. It is of Scottish origin and consists of stripes of various colors and widths against a solid ground, denoting a particular family lineage. The school's founder, Andrew Carnegie, was born in Dunfermline, Scotland, in 1835. Carnegie came to the United States in 1848 and founded Carnegie Technical Schools in Pittsburgh in 1900.

The Scottish terrier mascot performer sports Carnegie tartan attire, while the graphic mascot is wearing a plaid scarf around its neck. So what's the difference between tartan and plaid?

Tartan Facts

The Scottish terrier mascot performer sports Carnegie tartan attire, while the graphic mascot is wearing a plaid scarf around its neck. So what's the difference between tartan and plaid?

You'll know it's a tartan if...

• "It's a check or pattern in a variety of colours in woven fabric in which bands of colour are repeated in equal proportion in warp (running lengthwise) and weft (running across)."

• "Each stripe of the warp crosses every stripe of the weft, so when vertical and horizontal stripes of the same color cross, the result is solid color at the point of intersection."

• "The arrangement of colored threads is the same in the warp as in the weft."

You can find our official tartan on various items in the
University Store
.

Source: "Tartan: Romancing the Plaid," by Jeffrey Banks and Doria De La Chapelle

Official Mascot?

More than a century after Carnegie Mellon University opened its doors, an official mascot finally made its mark.

Tartan Facts

Official Mascot?

More than a century after Carnegie Mellon University opened its doors, an official mascot finally made its mark. Although students have dressed as a Scottish terrier — typically referred to as Scotty — for 50 years, it wasn't until 2007 that Carnegie Mellon officially welcomed the Scottish terrier as the university's first mascot.

In keeping with tradition, students, faculty, staff and alumni voted to name the new official mascot Scotty. But it's not just the costumed mascot that voters named. The live dog is also known as Scotty to the Carnegie Mellon community.

Student-Athlete Alumni Mentoring Program

Student-Athlete Alumni Mentoring Program

Carnegie Mellon Athletics is focused on developing leaders. Our ambition is for our student-athletes to take the skills and abilities developed as members of our intercollegiate athletics program into the broader world to lead meaningful lives while impacting society in profound ways. The Carnegie Mellon Student-Athlete Alumni Mentoring Program was created as a platform to foster relationships between past and present student-athletes to provide guidance, wisdom and opportunities to the current generation of Tartans.

The Carnegie Mellon Student-Athlete Alumni Mentoring Program will connect our world-class students and alumni in professional-based mentoring relationships. With a mentoring-specific software platform to guide the connections and communication, the mentoring program is designed to help current student-athletes develop an advantage as they prepare for careers, and to provide student-athlete alumni with the opportunity to stay connected with the Tartan community in a meaningful way.

Highmark Center for Health, Wellness and Athletics

Highmark Center for Health, Wellness and Athletics

The Highmark Center for Health, Wellness and Athletics opened in August 2024 and is home to varsity athletics. The building has a main arena which will be used for varsity basketball and varsity volleyball, as well as club sports, intramurals, physical education and other programs. There is also a second gymnasium for the entire campus community, a turf fieldhouse with running lanes and batting cages, and an impressive sports performance space that includes the varsity weight room and athletic training suite. There is also a intercollegiate golf training area with three virtual training screens.

Additionally, there are individual team locker rooms for each sport, a student-athlete lounge, and staff offices.

Carnegie Mellon University Athletics has received a $150,000 grant from an anonymous charitable organization to support and expand inclusive leadership development, mentoring, mental skills programming, and networking opportunities for Carnegie Mellon student-athletes.

Tartans Continue Academic Excellence Through Fall Semester

January 15, 2026

The fall athletics season was highlighted by four team NCAA Championship appearances and six nationally-ranked winter and spring teams, while the Tartans continued to excel in the classroom. An impressive 156 student-athletes achieved a perfect 4.0 GPA, and 67% earned a GPA of 3.50 or higher.

Arts & Entertainment Management Website

Impact Powered by Creativity
CMU’s College of Fine Arts and Heinz College of Information Systems and Public Policy jointly offer the Master of Arts Management (MAM) and Master of Entertainment Industry Management (MEIM) to create analytical and entrepreneurial leaders in the fields of visual arts, performing arts, film, television and interactive media. Through coursework and real-world experiential learning opportunities with industry leaders, these two-year master’s degree programs address the ways the creative industries are being transformed in a digital world.
Arts & Entertainment Management Degrees

Arts & Entertainment Management Website

Arts. Analytics. Action.

The
Master of Arts Management (MAM) program
centers on the intersection of people, policy and technology with an arts focus. Courses in analytics and quantitative management train students to navigate the rapidly changing arts economy of the 21st century, providing a skill set that arts organizations need and eagerly seek. MAM is the ideal fit for students seeking careers across the arts sector in museums, galleries, performing arts venues, foundations and nonprofits.

Arts & Entertainment Management

MAM is the ideal fit for students seeking careers across the arts sector in museums, galleries, performing arts venues, foundations and nonprofits. Our alumni are managers, marketers, fundraisers, analysts, advocates and leaders for arts organizations of all sizes.

Great Stories Need Great Leaders
With the dual-city
Master of Entertainment Industry Management (MEIM) program
, students spend their first year in Pittsburgh and their second year working in the industry in Los Angeles. In addition, students take part in cohort trips to film festivals including Sundance, SXSW and Cannes. Providing greater quantitative management and strategic skills than a film school and more entertainment-relevant coursework and experiences than a business school, MEIM prepares graduates to have an impact on development, marketing, production, distribution and strategy at all levels across a global entertainment marketplace.

CFA Photography

CFA Photography

CFA Photography Website

Make Powerful Photographs in an Image-Saturated World
Create more than just a good picture. The CFA Photography interdisciplinary courses and minor can help you use photography as a form of personal expression and cultural communication. Learn fundamentals and develop your artistic approach as you learn to communicate meaning through image-making.
Our courses play to each instructor's innate strengths. Learn in the real world, in real time with photography professionals offering a rich variety of styles, media and techniques.
CFA Dean's Office Minors

CFA Photography Website

From Darkroom to Digital

CFA Photography exposes you to a wide range of image-making approaches: traditional film, non-silver processes, modern digital technologies, medium and large format photography, and a unique assortment of unconventional — and sometimes unusual — cameras. Find your own style as you explore a fusion of vintage and state-of-the-art photography.
Our core curriculum provides a solid foundation for anyone wanting to grow as an image-maker.

Design, Create, Make in the Real World

You won't just do one step in the process. You'll learn all the parts from conception to completion, providing you with a better understanding of what is feasible and making you a more empathetic designer.

School of Art

School of Art

School of Art Website

The Place for Art, Technology and Theory
At the Carnegie Mellon University
School of Art
, students begin by asking bold questions. Here, artists challenge norms, cross disciplines and experiment with new approaches, grounded in conceptual thinking and the resources of a top-ranked research university. With only 50 undergraduate and six graduate students each year, the school fosters an intimate community where internationally recognized faculty challenge and support students to expand their thinking as artists.
School of Art Degrees

School of Art Website

Artmaking as a Vital Intellectual Pursuit

Art at CMU is a way of engaging with the world. The graduate program’s unique three-year structure is designed to provide the time and resources for in-depth multidisciplinary research. Undergraduate students choose between two degree programs, each designed to support individual paths while building fluency in traditional media, critical studies and emerging technologies. Peer and faculty feedback, hands-on studio exploration and 24-hour studio access empower students to deeply explore their artistic practices.

Our programs are unified by a framework that contextualizes design, while also seeking to shape the future of the discipline and advance the field as it matures. Our students become "systems thinkers," able to see and solve complex problems in a globally connected and interdependent world. The career possibilities — and your potential to make an impact on the world — are limitless.

Home

About the college

Advanced Collaboration
®

Our world is changing faster, and its problems are bigger than ever.

Where knowledge once proceeded in a linear fashion from insight to insight, today its movement is startling and unpredictable. The once steady expansion of knowledge has turned exponential, and today new discoveries and information bombard us from every direction. This means that every moment we really know less and less compared with the information available to us.

The constant intersections of emerging voices and data at play in our everyday lives cause new, complex issues to emerge, challenging the conventional modes of working and demanding a new model for interdisciplinary initiatives.

Now more than ever, we must work together to survive and innovate.

Global impact

Home

About the college

Global impact

Since 2002, the College of Engineering has gained substantial experience in operating across the world. In doing so, we have concentrated our efforts on developing engagements to maximize the mutually beneficial impact for both the College and the communities we serve.

Major global engagements

Pittsburgh

Our Pittsburgh campus serves over 4,000 engineering students through nine academic departments, three major research institutes, and more than 20 center-scale research efforts.

CMU-Africa

Our location in Rwanda offers Master of Science (MS) degrees and operates a collaborative research center, start-up incubator, and the Afretec Network.

CMU Portugal

In Portugal, the College of Engineering offers dual Doctor of Philosophy degrees, affiliated Ph.D. programs, and advanced training programs. The college also funds large-scale and exploratory research projects, fosters company partnerships, and provides entrepreneurial support.

Silicon Valley

CMU-Silicon Valley offers Master of Science (MS) degrees through the Electrical and Computer Engineering Department, Information Networking Institute, and Integrated Innovation Institute.

Afretec

About the college

Home

About the college

The College of Engineering at Carnegie Mellon is a renowned institution that is widely recognized for its excellence, innovation, and the significant impact its research has on society.

Our engineering program is designed to produce technically proficient and creative engineers who can provide cutting-edge solutions to global challenges.

We take pride in our commitment to interdisciplinary collaboration, bringing together experts from various fields, such as engineering, sciences, arts, and business, to achieve transformative outcomes.

Leadership

Global impact

Community Engagement and Outreach

Alumni engagement

Giving to the College of Engineering

Advanced collaboration

World-renowned

The College of Engineering has a long history of excellence. Our people are the driving force behind our success as one of the top engineering schools in the world, and our faculty, staff, students, and alumni have earned recognition in a variety of fields. From earning Nobel Prizes and Turing Awards to being named National Academies fellows, Carnegie Mellon Engineers continue to drive innovation, shape policy, and pave the way to a better future for all.

Home

Education

Graduate studies

Graduate programs

The College of Engineering provides a range of graduate programs that are both traditional and interdisciplinary. The programs are designed to foster a maker ecosystem where students and faculty from different disciplines collaborate to create solutions to complex problems in industry, government, and academia.

Graduates of these programs have excellent prospects in various fields, including industry, government, academia, and the corporate world. The college’s global alumni network is transforming the engineering profession by using an authentic interdisciplinary approach to problem-solving, which is the hallmark of Carnegie Mellon. Every day, our engineers are making a significant impact.

Home

News

Rethinking the environmental impact of automotive inspections

by
Hillary Roman

New findings from Carnegie Mellon challenge assumptions about how safety regulations change driving behavior.

Many states enforce vehicle inspection laws to reduce traffic accidents, congestion, and harmful emissions from older cars. Regulatory analysis may assume keeping older cars on the road translates to a proportional surge in overall driving and fuel consumption. However,
new research from Carnegie Mellon University
reveals that while fleet size does grow after mandatory safety inspections are removed, travel and fuel consumption do not grow proportionally.

Source:
From U.S. Government Accountability Office and U.S, Census Bureau

Maps of the year that each state implemented safety inspections (left) and the year that each state removed safety inspections (right). States colored gray in both the left and right panels never implemented safety inspection programs; states colored gray in the right panel do not have a year that safety inspections ended, either because they never started or because they started but never ended.

retrieval_text:
Rethinking the environmental impact of automotive inspections

These maps exclude Alaska and Hawaii; Alaska has never had safety inspections; Hawaii began safety inspections in 1961, and they are still in place. The District of Columbia had safety inspections from 1939 to 2009.

Researchers Connor Forsythe, Akshaya Jha,
Jeremy Michalek
, and
Kate Whitefoot
studied how mandatory vehicle inspection policies shape total driving habits and environmental impacts. They compiled 47 years of U.S. Federal Highway Administration data across all 50 states tracking statewide vehicle registrations, vehicle miles traveled, gasoline usage, and road mileage. Leveraging the staggered termination of mandatory safety inspection programs across various states from 1970 to 2017, the researchers used a difference-in-differences model to show that while removing these policies does increase overall fleet size by roughly 5%, the empirical evidence does not suggest similar growth in total miles driven or gasoline consumed.

“As safety inspections were removed, it seems that people kept old cars around longer before scrapping them but didn’t drive them as much,” says Michalek.

Fleet growth does not equal more traffic

attributes.description: New findings from Carnegie Mellon challenge assumptions about how safety regulations change driving behavior.

retrieval_text:
Rethinking the environmental impact of automotive inspections

Fleet growth does not equal more traffic

The removal of mandatory vehicle inspection laws predictably results in an increase in total car ownership. One reason for this effect may be that more people retain an old car that would have otherwise required expensive repairs to remain drivable.

Strikingly, however, the authors found that increased fleet size did not have a proportional effect on driving behavior. The authors implemented an instrumental variables framework to measure how changes in fleet sizes alter travel distance and fuel usage. They compared miles driven and gas consumed in states with mandatory inspections and states without.

While this finding contradicts some policymakers’ assumptions, it is logically consistent: change in the number of vehicles owned would not necessarily impact driver travel routines. It’s possible that people kept older cars longer but mainly used them as backups to their primary vehicles.

Prior empirical research on how automotive policy affects the externality costs of fleet travel distance and fuel use. Bold text and arrows highlight the factors examined in this study.

A $90 billion overestimate

retrieval_text:
AI helps pathologists find signs of preeclampsia, advancing diagnosis and treatment

Home

News

AI helps pathologists find signs of preeclampsia, advancing diagnosis and treatment

by
Kaitlyn Landram

By revealing the biological features behind its decision, a new AI model from Jon Cagan and Phil LeDuc working with Liron Pantanowitz at UPMC helps pathologists detect signs of preeclampsia while building trust in AI-assisted diagnosis.

You might also like...

Predictive placentas: Using AI to protect mothers’ future pregnancies

Preeclampsia is one of the leading causes of pregnancy-related death. Even after a healthy delivery, mom and baby can go home only to show signs of postpartum hypertensive disorder days or weeks later.

Examining the placenta after delivery can provide important clues about complications that occurred during pregnancy and identify future risk. One such clue is decidual vasculopathy, a disease of the material blood vessels in the placenta that is commonly associated with postpartum preeclampsia. However, there is a profound shortage of perinatal pathologists trained to conduct routine placenta screenings, meaning that today less than 20% of placentas are screened in the United States after delivery.

retrieval_text:
AI helps pathologists find signs of preeclampsia, advancing diagnosis and treatment

To streamline this process with the hope that one day all placentas are reviewed by pathologists for signs of disease, researchers in the
Department of Mechanical Engineering
at Carnegie Mellon University and the Department of Pathology at UPMC have developed a machine learning algorithm that can quickly identify placentas with notable biomarkers and flag cases that may require further review from a specialized pathologist.

“Screening placentas is a bit like playing
Where’s Waldo
,” said Mangalam Sahai, first author of the research paper published in
npj Digital Medicine
, “We are looking for five diseased blood vessels in a sea of three to four thousand very similar looking vessels.”

One of the biological differences pathologists look for involves extravillous trophoblast cells (EVT), cells that help remodel the maternal blood vessels to make sure that enough blood is reaching the placenta and the developing fetus. In vessels affected by decidual vasculopathy, the organization of these cells relative to red blood cells changes.

In vessels affected by decidual vasculopathy, the organization of these cells relative to red blood cells changes. The researchers’ first step was, therefore, to use stain-dependent light transmittance properties of EVT and red blood cells within images of placental vessels to identify their spatial organization.

This is a bit like comparing two types of trail mix: both contain the same ingredients, but in different proportions. By looking at the relative amount of each ingredient, you can distinguish one mix from the other. Similarly, the model looks at the relative distribution of EVTs and red blood cells within a vessel to distinguish healthy from diseased vessels. The algorithm converts those patterns into a standardized score that indicates how typical or unusual the cell organization is. Rather than simply labeling a vessel as “diseased” or “healthy,” the team’s model stands out because of a third, unique step that calculates what the researchers call a morphology separation score. This score compares the relative distributions of EVTs and red blood cells within each vessel.

Selling sunshine

by
Hillary Roman

New research shows how advances in renewable energy storage will impact market incentives.

How renewables change the energy market

Governments worldwide rely on increasing solar and wind energy as they pivot toward low-emission energy grids. The shift away from fossil fuels is a net benefit, but not without challenges. On sunny afternoons and windy evenings, grid operators must manage electricity surges that far exceed consumer demand. When this occurs, oversupply forces wholesale electricity prices down to zero or even below, compelling power companies to turn off clean energy generators. Unlike most market commodities, the power grid can be physically damaged by a supply flood.

To avoid damaging equipment without throwing away renewable power, grid operators need a way to absorb these sudden energy floods.

In traditional markets, sellers get paid for providing goods. However, electricity has a unique physical constraint: the power grid must maintain a precise balance between supply and demand at all times to avoid blackouts or damaged equipment.

retrieval_text:
Selling sunshine

In their research, recently published in
Current Sustainable/Renewable Energy Reports
,
Sioshansi and Yagi describe two kinds of modern energy storage: sodium-sulfur (NaS) batteries that electrochemically store energy through the reactions between sodium and sulfur, and TES systems that convert electricity into thermal energy and store it as a heated medium, typically molten salt.

Thermal energy storage

NaS and TES carry different trade-offs. NaS batteries have a higher per-unit energy capacity cost (how much energy a fully charged device can hold). However, they are highly efficient, operating at about 90% round-trip efficiency, meaning that NaS batteries lose only 10% of the stored energy in the conversion and discharging processes. TES systems, on the other hand, have lower per-unit energy capacity cost, but they are far less efficient. Their round-trip efficiency is only about 41%, meaning roughly 59% of the input energy is lost as waste heat.

Despite such large efficiency losses, TES systems offer several major advantages. Unlike chemical batteries, thermal equipment has flexible scalability that allows systems to absorb excess power faster than they discharge it.

Unlike chemical batteries, thermal equipment has flexible scalability that allows systems to absorb excess power faster than they discharge it. Rapid charging capability makes these systems better equipped to handle sudden generation surges on particularly sunny or windy days.

TES systems can also be retrofitted onto retired coal and natural gas infrastructure with relative ease, leveraging existing grid connections and steam turbines. NaS battery storage facilities, however, assume a much higher cost as they require specialized electrochemical cells and power-conversion hardware that are more expensive to scale.

Future energy markets and policy implications

The authors model how energy storage solutions may develop using Japan’s identified solar and wind targets for the years 2030 and 2050.

The authors predict that as renewable energy grows, the number of hours per day with near-zero energy prices will increase by 2030, but not significantly. Under these conditions, NaS batteries remain the superior choice due to high round-trip efficiency for moderate need.

by
Kaitlyn Landram

Carnegie Mellon researchers are using explainable AI to uncover patterns hidden in centuries old paintings, to give experts a new tool for investigating who may have painted them.

Pictured above:

Jon Cagan, J. Kenneth Moritz, Andrés Arias-Rosales, Arthur K. Wheelock Jr., and Phil LeDuc at the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC, in front of the Rembrandt painting, “A Polish Nobleman.”

A few hundred years ago, authenticating whether a painting was created by a master like Rembrandt, or a talented copy-cat, was dependent only on the trained eye of an expert. Then, new tools like X-rays and infrared imaging allowed curators to see beneath the surface of a painting and analyze details invisible to the human eye.

Now, researchers at Carnegie Mellon University are exploring how artificial intelligence can work alongside human experts to add another layer of evidence towards the unsolved mysteries in art attribution.

Seeing Rembrandt through the eyes of a machine

Now, researchers at Carnegie Mellon University are exploring how artificial intelligence can work alongside human experts to add another layer of evidence towards the unsolved mysteries in art attribution.

In work published in the
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
and led by Mechanical Engineering Professors Phil LeDuc and Jon Cagan, alongside alumnus Andrés Arias-Rosales and renowned Rembrandt scholar Arthur Wheelock Jr., the researchers have developed an AI framework that can examine a painting for visual patterns associated with the work of Rembrandt to help experts make the final call on a painting’s authenticity.

Attributing a painting to an artist like Rembrandt is no easy task. Experts consider everything from historical documents to the artist’s subject matter, his varied styles of painting throughout the course of his career, including brushwork and the types of paints and supports he used. On top of that, they must keep in mind that Rembrandt’s pupils and assistants may have sometimes painted alongside him and that later restorers may have changed and added elements to Rembrandt’s compositions.

retrieval_text:
Seeing Rembrandt through the eyes of a machine

“We wanted to understand Rembrandt through the eyes of a world-class expert, then understand it through the eyes of ‘the machine,’ our AI approach, and bring those together.”

Prior to diving into developing the new AI tools, it was crucial for the team to first go to the National Gallery of Art, DC, to study Rembrandt paintings and engage in in-depth discussions about the artist, his style and technique, and the questions and challenges surrounding his work.

The team then asked whether an AI approach could distinguish Rembrandt from paintings by artists whose work resembles that of the master. The team carefully curated a dataset of more than 1,300 high-resolution digitized images of paintings including 311 Rembrandts that were used for the AI analysis.

The AI model learned to identify statistical patterns across characteristics such as edges, color, light distribution, and visible brushstrokes to produce a score estimating how strongly a painting aligns with the patterns shown in Rembrandt’s work. When the model was highly confident, it classified paintings with 95.8% accuracy.

“Experts need to understand how the AI model/algorithm came to its decision,” said Cagan. “That is critical in successful human-AI collaboration, so we needed to make sure the algorithm could expose which areas of the painting influenced the algorithm’s conclusion.”

To do so, the AI approach classifies a painting as either Rembrandt or not, provides carefully calibrated probabilities and confidence scores, and generates visualizations that emphasize the painting areas and details that had the strongest influence in the AI-based classification. This becomes a useful tool for curators as they can focus on specific details within the painting that they may have otherwise overlooked. For example, if the AI was repeatedly highlighting the hands with a low score, suggesting that they likely weren’t painted by Rembrandt, the researchers can digitally remove them from consideration and ask the model to classify it again.

retrieval_text:
History

History

Founder Spotlight

A self-educated "working boy," Andrew Carnegie emigrated from Scotland in 1848 and settled in Pittsburgh, Pa. Attending night school and borrowing books, Carnegie went from factory worker in a textile mill to successful entrepreneur and industrialist. He rose to prominence by founding what became the world's largest steel producing company by the end of the 19th century.
"My heart is in the work," he stated, which would become part of the school's official motto.
At one point the richest man in the world, Carnegie once said, "To die rich is to die disgraced." He turned his attention to writing, social activism and philanthropy, determined to establish educational opportunities for the general public where few existed.

CMU's Origin

1900: Initial Funding for Carnegie Technical Schools

In 1900, Andrew Carnegie donated $1 million to the city of Pittsburgh, envisioning a school where working-class men and women of Pittsburgh could learn practical skills, trades and crafts that would enhance their careers, lives and communities.

The Carnegie Technical Schools offered two- and three-year certificates in the arts as well as in engineering disciplines and included a college for women, Margaret Morrison Carnegie College.

Initial number of students

The first Carnegie Technical Schools class was admitted in 1906.

Degrees Introduced

1912: Carnegie Tech Grants Bachelor's Degrees

Soon faced with the demand for baccalaureate programs, Carnegie Technical Schools changed its name to the Carnegie Institute of Technology, or "Carnegie Tech", and began offering bachelor's degrees through its College of Engineering and College of Fine Arts.
Carnegie Tech set the groundwork for a research institution, recruiting leading scientists, offering sponsored fellowships with government and industry leaders and pioneering nontraditional interdisciplinary research, which brought together physicists, chemists and metallurgists, for example. Interdisciplinary research would become the hallmark of Carnegie Mellon research. In 1919, the first doctorate (in civil engineering) was awarded to Mao Yisheng, a student from China.

CMU's Global Leadership

In its 115 years, Carnegie Mellon has soared to national and international leadership in higher education and research. A birthplace of innovation since its founding, it continues to be known for innovation, for solving real-world problems and for interdisciplinary collaboration. Its alumni can be found across the globe — from Tony Award winners to Nobel Prize and Turing Award winners, from CEOs to entrepreneurs, from professors to artists.
In the 2000s, in response to demand for expanded international educational opportunities, Carnegie Mellon began offering degree programs outside of Pittsburgh.

The Academy of Television Arts and Sciences honors individuals for their artistic, educational and technical achievements in the television industry. Awards shared by two or more alumni have been counted once.

Rankings

College and university rankings continue to proliferate, but their value to individuals and to the institutions remains a subject of some debate. Some rankings are designed purely for entertainment, little more than internet photo galleries. Others make a more serious effort at collecting information.
Even where rankings do collect objective statistics such as test scores or costs, the choice of which factors to include in a ranking, and how those factors are weighted, remains subjective. The effects of those methodologies, and the reasons for those choices, are not always readily apparent.
For prospective students, families, potential staff and faculty who are deciding whether to invest time and resources in an institution, it is essential that you decide what factors are important to your success and the outcomes you seek.

Traditions

Traditions

Connected to the Past, Shaping the Future
At Carnegie Mellon University (CMU), traditions are more than just events — they're a celebration of our bold and collaborative community. Some commemorate the Scottish heritage of our founder, Andrew Carnegie, while others originate from previous CMU students. These hallmark experiences help create the fabric of the university, building a tight-knit campus with a creative, quirky spirit.
From the distinctive sounds of the
Carnegie Mellon Pipes and Drums
to the joyful energy of
Spring Carnival
, our traditions embody our fearless, visionary spirit, honor our rich history and pave the way for an extraordinary future.
Explore the many annual traditions and programs where the entire CMU community comes together to connect, engage and unleash their
Tartan pride
.

The Fence at CMU

Have a message for campus? Paint it on the Fence, a tradition that made the original structure the most painted object in the world. Help our current Fence retake that title.

Learn About the Fence

Some commemorate the Scottish heritage of our founder, Andrew Carnegie, while others originate from previous CMU students. These hallmark experiences help create the fabric of the university, building a tight-knit campus with a creative, quirky spirit.
From the distinctive sounds of the
Carnegie Mellon Pipes and Drums
to the joyful energy of
Spring Carnival
, our traditions embody our fearless, visionary spirit, honor our rich history and pave the way for an extraordinary future.
Explore the many annual traditions and programs where the entire CMU community comes together to connect, engage and unleash their
Tartan pride
.

The Fence at CMU

Have a message for campus? Paint it on the Fence, a tradition that made the original structure the most painted object in the world. Help our current Fence retake that title.

Vision, Mission and Values

Vision, Mission and Values

Empowering the Next Generation of World-Changers
Carnegie Mellon University’s vision, mission and values guide us in providing an exceptional educational experience and creating a diverse community of creators, inventors and leaders. See how they help us cultivate an open, cooperative culture that values entrepreneurial thinking and addresses real-world problems.
Vision
Carnegie Mellon University will have a transformative impact on society through continual innovation in education, research, creativity and entrepreneurship.
Mission
To create a transformative educational experience for students focused on deep disciplinary knowledge; problem-solving; leadership, communication and interpersonal skills; and personal health and well-being.
To cultivate a transformative university community committed to (a) attracting and retaining diverse, world-class talent; (b) creating a collaborative environment open to the free exchange of ideas, where research, creativity, innovation and entrepreneurship can flourish; and (c) ensuring individuals can achieve their full potential.
To impact society in a transformative way — regionally, nationally and globally — by engaging with partners outside the traditional borders of the university campus.

Vision, Mission and Values

A History of Work that Matters

In 1900, philanthropist Andrew Carnegie donated $1 million to found a school where students from all backgrounds could gain skills to uplift their careers and communities. Over 100 years later, CMU continues that spirit as a global leader in education and research.

Learn More About CMU's History

Commitment to Belonging

Ranging perspectives and experiences catalyze CMU’s passionate and uninhibited spirit. That’s why we cultivate an environment with educational access and community engagement so all feel welcomed, supported and empowered to achieve their full potential.

Planning for CMU’s Future
CMU’s Strategic Framework provides a vision to drive the university's mission through education, research and global impact. Learn about the plan’s accomplishments and how we are updating it to meet our future endeavors and goals.
Learn About Our Strategic Framework

Interdisciplinary Programs

Interdisciplinary Programs at Carnegie Mellon

Pursue Your Passions Without Boundaries
At Carnegie Mellon University, we cross traditional boundaries and shatter academic silos. Our undergraduate and graduate levels empower you to follow your intellectual curiosities wherever they lead — from the latest computational biology research to next-gen entertainment technology marvels.
Our interdisciplinary DNA encourages you to seek excellence, challenge assumptions and forge creative discoveries. Here, you'll develop the integrative mindset to achieve more than you ever thought possible — and even
reach for the moon
.

BXA Intercollege Degree Programs

Blend analytical study and creative training with CMU’s BXA Intercollege Degree Programs. Take courses in both the College of Fine Arts and other disciplines to fuse your passions, from computer science and engineering to humanities and science.

Explore CMU's BXA Programs

Integrative Design, Arts and Technology Network (IDeATe)

Fuse technology with artistic expression with an interdisciplinary minor from IDeATe. Gain expertise across engineering, fine arts, humanities, sciences, computer science and business fields as you study topics such as game design, intelligent environments and immersive technologies.

Learn About IDeATe Minors

Frequently Asked Questions About Interdisciplinary Studies

By integrating multiple areas of study into your undergraduate or graduate program, you gain creative, technical and practical skills that position you to drive innovation across disciplines in unique ways. Benefits to interdisciplinary studies include:
Pursuing multiple interests by choosing areas that interest you most
Accessing diverse expert insights and methodologies across CMU disciplines
Following your intellectual curiosity to new or more efficient solutions
Learning to communicate and collaborate with people with different academic backgrounds
Building integrative problem-solving abilities prized by employers

You can complete most CMU interdisciplinary programs within the same timeframe as traditional undergraduate or graduate programs. The key difference lies in the flexibility to customize your academic path. Choose courses from multiple departments or colleges as you fulfill your degree requirements.
Undergraduate students: If you are adding a double major or an additional major to create an interdisciplinary experience, be sure to talk to an academic advisor.

CMU - Conference & Event Services - Carnegie Mellon University

One-Stop Shop

Conference & Event Services takes pride in delivering professional and organized events. With over 40 years of combined event planning experience, we are your one-stop shop for catering, room reservations, summer campus housing, hotel accommodations, audio/visual, parking, web registration and many more customized services. Our staff works closely with you to ensure your next conference, meeting, summer camp or event is specially tailored to accommodate your needs.

We have established strong relationships with campus service providers and local businesses (i.e., hotels, transportation, rental companies, etc.) who work with us to create a unique event. To ensure a seamless experience, we are your single point of contact throughout the planning process.

Book your next event with confidence, and you will be able to focus on the program while we take care of all of the details. Your effortless event begins with Conference & Event Services.

Academics

Academics at Dietrich College of Humanities and Social Sciences

Humanities and social sciences students at Carnegie Mellon University publish poetry and analyze brain scans, study abroad in Costa Rican rain forests and mentor Pittsburgh K-12 students. Forge your academic and personal path at Dietrich College.
What Sets Dietrich College’s Academics Apart

Alumni News

Congratulations to all the undergraduates who made the
Fall 2025 Dietrich College Dean’s List
!

January 2026
Kat Tsai
(CFA 2018, DC 2019) earned a spot on 2026 Forbes’ 30 Under 30 list in the
Art & Style category
, while
Sid Malladi
(DC 2018) and
Rameez Remsudeen
(DC 2018) share a spot in the
Finance category
.
John Edwards
(DC 1997) has written a children's book, "
Our Phones Left Home
". You can
follow his journey on Instagram
.
Staten Rector
(CMU 2027) published the article “
Taiwan: democratic David in 21st century east Asia
” in the journal Frontiers In Political Science. The piece began as a final project for the International Relations course, then was later developed into a full research report through the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy & Technology’s Undergraduate Research for Credit course.
In its 12th year celebrating academic and athletic achievement on Reading Day,
the Carnegie Mellon Department of Athletics honored 34 of the highest-achieving juniors and seniors across all colleges and athletics teams
.

. Stoken is now a client partner at Randstad Digital.

Joshua Ingram

,

the executive director of the national
Chinese Language Teachers Association
(CLTA), worked with her ACTFL/CLTA 2022 conference committee to run a successful ACTFL/CLTA 2022 annual convention program in Boston, November 18-21. During the conference, Wu presented her paper titled “Incorporating Outreach and Advocacy Activities into a DEI CFL Curriculum” at the ACTFL 2022 convention. Wu also delivered opening remarks at the first “National Chinese EXPO of Student Works” showcase that boasted more than 200 student works with more than 4,000 students from 47 states and Canada.
Wu also held the Chinese Culture Night Showcase along with students from her class “Topics in Chinese Language, Culture and Society” (82-139). During the event, participants took advantage of karaoke, Taichi and dances, puppetry, Chinese dress and photos, calligraphy and bookmarks, Chinese knotting and Chinese games. All proceeds from the event went to benefit Kesem-CMU, an organization dedicated to providing year-round support for children affected by a parental cancer.

Faculty Spotlight: Amber Hedquist

Oct 21, 2026

Faculty Spotlight: Amber Hedquist

By Stefanie Johndrow

Email Stefanie Johndrow

Amber Hedquist
is an assistant teaching professor and associate director of professional and technical writing programs in Carnegie Mellon University’s Department of English in the Dietrich College of Humanities and Social Sciences. Her research and teaching focus is on technical and professional communication, user experience (UX), community-engaged research and emerging technologies
Tell me about your scholarly work.
I specialize in technical and professional communication (TPC), and my research investigates how people communicate and collaborate. Specifically, I study how people work together across disciplines, technologies, institutions and communities, with particular attention to the communication practices and technologies that influence and scaffold that work.
When describing my research, I reference Pam Estes Brewer’s characterization of collaboration as complex work that is “facilitated by many choices in both structure and technology.” Much of my research is inspired by those choices, leading to questions such as: How do teams coordinate their work? How do researchers build relationships with communities? How can emerging technologies support collaborative work?

To answer these questions, I study the practices, methods and tools that help people work together on complex problems.

My contribution to technical and professional communication is developing methods, frameworks and heuristics that help people navigate collaborative work.

in the workplace.

a framework for building reciprocity
in community-engaged research.

rhetorical approaches to drafting recruitment materials

How did you become interested in this topic?
Throughout my career in higher education, my roles have included public affairs management, UX research, research administration, project management and teaching. Each role involved working in interdisciplinary teams, requiring careful attention to how people communicate and make decisions. retrieval_text:
Faculty Spotlight: Amber Hedquist

My work with
WaterSIMmersive
is a great example. This National Science Foundation‑funded project is focused on developing museum exhibits about water in Arizona to improve environmental action. Our team collaborated with rural, urban and tribal communities across the state to understand their goals for the exhibit and to design experiences that reflected their knowledge, values and relationships with water. The work required responsive and reciprocal communication: listening carefully, adapting our processes and building exhibit components that honored diverse perspectives. My team and I were attentive to the rhetorical, cultural and logistical decisions that shape interdisciplinary collaboration, and we worked deliberately to build processes grounded in care, respect and reciprocity.
What are you most excited to accomplish as a faculty member at CMU?
I am joining a CMU program with a strong history of leadership in professional and technical writing. I want to build on that foundation. My goals fall into three areas: programmatic leadership, research and teaching.

Faculty Spotlight: Amber Hedquist

What are your goals for the next generation of scholars?
To say I am inspired by CMU students is an understatement. Their curiosity, creativity and ambition make me equally ambitious about what they can accomplish. I have two goals in particular for them:
Embrace that Everyone is a Writer.
Everyone at CMU is a writer. Whatever their field, students need to communicate ideas, articulate their contributions and collaborate with others. My goal is for students to recognize the importance of developing their writing skills and to actively seek out courses and opportunities that strengthen their writing.

Recognize Writing as Decision Making.
Writing is a series of decisions, and decisions have consequences. Choices about authorship, genre, audience, language and purpose shape reach and impact. Thus, I want students to recognize writing as a significant responsibility.
Finally, inspired by “Ted Lasso,” my favorite show, I want the next generation of scholars to stay curious. Curiosity creates the conditions for creative problem solving and challenging assumptions. In short, curiosity catalyzes change. I cannot wait to see what CMU students imagine, question and build.

How to Separate Cause From Coincidence

The Causal Inference Working Group, hosted by the Dietrich College Department of Statistics & Data Science, leads to real-world impacts.

By Jason Bittel

Email Jason Bittel

One month, coffee is bad for you. The next, it’s a superfood. Similarly, butter, eggs, wine and a host of other products have gone from villain to hero and back again. And while stories like these grab many headlines, correlation-heavy studies can also erode the public’s trust in science altogether.
But at Carnegie Mellon University’s Dietrich College of Humanities and Social Sciences, an interdisciplinary group of researchers is working to design studies that don’t just find patterns and correlations — they actually infer causation. And this cohort has already generated exciting, new research across a wide range of topics, from criminal justice and healthcare to social services and human rights.

Zach Branson

“The correlation-doesn’t-imply-causation line is perhaps the greatest public relations thing that anyone’s ever done for statistics,” said
Zach Branson
, an associate teaching professor and assistant director of the undergraduate program for the
Department of Statistics & Data Science
. “But it does also make some people think that you can never get a causal inference.”
In fact, researchers are getting better at proving causation all the time, and new tools, such as machine learning and artificial intelligence, are helping them in that quest. Since 2016, the Statistics & Data Science Department has looked to serve as an incubator for this type of work by hosting something called the
Causal Inference Working Group
.
“Broadly speaking, this is a group of faculty and graduate students who are all interested in causal inference from a statistical perspective,” said Branson.

The group meets weekly and works to develop statistical and computational methods that help researchers move beyond correlation and toward evidence they can use with more confidence. Sometimes, a researcher will present on an interesting new paper published in the field, while other times, a member will come to the group looking for advice on a study or experiment that is already taking place.

“Causal inference is something that comes up everywhere,” said
Eli Ben-Michael
, an assistant professor in the Department of Statistics & Data Science and Heinz College. “They care about it in economics, and in medicine, and anywhere where you want to compare two groups and make sure the only thing that’s different is the thing we actually care about.”
Why Causation Matters
Edward Kennedy
, professor in the Department of Statistics & Data Science and co-founder of the working group, helps build tools that researchers can use to find causal inference out in the real world.

Siva Balakrishnan, working group participant

He’s been part of massive experiments at Facebook, Meta and Instagram that looked at how algorithms can affect people’s consumption of social media, and what that might mean for, say, political polarization. Interestingly,
one study published in the journal Nature in 2023
found that echo chambers don’t actually cause polarization.
“Which was surprising,” Kennedy said.

Interestingly,
one study published in the journal Nature in 2023
found that echo chambers don’t actually cause polarization.
“Which was surprising,” Kennedy said.
However, there’s a chance that the causal inference models he developed for that suite of research might be more useful in detecting causality in much smaller subsets of participants. Interestingly, these so-called “personalized causal effects” — or situations where the overall group does not show causality, but subgroups within the whole do — are one of the ways machine learning can help researchers discover new insights that would have been invisible before.
“This comes up a lot in medicine, where researchers may want to try to tailor medical decisions to certain kinds of people,” said Kennedy. “For instance, we know that some drugs don’t work on some types of people.”
Rather than dismissing the drug or treatment altogether, causal inference methods can help researchers hone in on the populations that can best use them.
“We’re getting good at finding subtle stories in the data you might miss with more classical methods,” he said.

Another Ph.D. student,
Lorenzo Testa
, showed that the same data can yield substantially different conclusions about how genes act in the mouse and human brains, as well as in human breast cancer tissues, depending on how the data is handled — a problem Testa was able to account for using, you guessed it, causal inference.
“So I always tell students, I know these examples can seem theoretical, but this can also be life and death,” said Branson.
From to economics and criminal justice to determining whether public policies actually achieve the results they intend or how cancer is detected, causal inference is everywhere.
“The Causal Inference Working Group is a wonderful example of interdisciplinary research that has momentous societal impact,” said
Rebecca Nugent
, the Stephen E. and Joyce Fienberg Professor and head of the Department of Statistics & Data Science. “These faculty also have developed foundational and cutting-edge courses in causal theory, methods and applications for undergraduate students, graduate students and working professionals that are in constant demand.”

Dietrich College of Humanities and Social Sciences

Dreamers and Doers, Welcome
At Carnegie Mellon University's Dietrich College of Humanities and Social Sciences, students and faculty explore past and present human experiences to shape a better future.
The insights we gain and discoveries we make help us better understand our history and tackle modern-day challenges. As a student, you will be immersed in this environment from day one. Learn how you can graduate with the skills you need to investigate, solve problems and continually learn in our rapidly changing world.

Alumni Awards

Alumni Awards

The CMU Alumni Association proudly honors these members of the CMU community, all of whom have made an impact on their industries, their communities, their alma mater and others' lives around the world.
The annual Alumni Awards event brings alumni, students, faculty, staff and friends together to celebrate those receiving the Founders Medal for Outstanding Service and Exceptional Achievement, Alumni Achievement Awards, Alumni Service Awards and Recent Alumni Awards.

Explore photos from the 76th Alumni Awards:
Hover over the photo above to scroll through a photo gallery of the event.
View all honorees since 1950

2026 Alumni Awards

Carnegie Mellon University alumni are known for changing the world and this year’s 11 Alumni Award honorees are adding to that Tartan legacy.
Representing all seven colleges and schools, this year’s honorees are active in fields including computer science, AI and robotics, public service, manufacturing, national security, real estate and infrastructure, private equity and investment, construction, clinical research and environmental advocacy.
Meet the Recipients

retrieval_text:
Alumni Awards

Meet the Recipients

Award Categories

Founders Medal for Outstanding Service and Exceptional Achievement
The Founders Medal is presented to an alumnus/a in recognition of both a longstanding record of service to and support for Carnegie Mellon University, and a record of professional or vocational achievements that are truly exceptional and have brought honor and prestige to themselves and to CMU. All alumni are eligible for this award, including those who have received prior alumni honors from the university or one of its colleges, schools or departments.

Alumni Achievement Award
Awarded to an alumnus/a for exceptional accomplishment and leadership in the nominee's professional or vocational field, which brings distinction to themselves and honor to the university. The contribution(s) need not be publicly renowned but should represent important creative effort or accomplishment with significant impact and value.

Alumni Service Award
Presented to an alumnus/a for volunteer service to the university or any of its alumni organizations.

attributes.description: Carnegie Mellon University's annual Alumni Awards event brings alumni, students, faculty, staff and friends together to celebrate those receiving the Founders Medal for Outstanding Service and Exceptional Achievement, Alumni Achievement Awards, Alumni Service Awards and Recent Alumni Awards.

retrieval_text:
Alumni Awards

Alumni Service Award
Presented to an alumnus/a for volunteer service to the university or any of its alumni organizations. Several dimensions of service are considered, including breadth of service (service in multiple CMU volunteer roles), depth or longevity of service, and impact of volunteer service on the alumni organization and/or the university. Financial contributions are specifically excluded from consideration for this award, although volunteer service soliciting contributions on behalf of the university or service on CMU fundraising committees is applicable. This award does not consider volunteer service to non-CMU organizations. Similarly, Carnegie Mellon employees or those alumni with business relationships to the university are not eligible on the basis of their employment duties or business services.

Recent Alumni Awards
Recent Alumni Achievement Award:
Awarded to an alumnus/a who received either a graduate or undergraduate degree from Carnegie Mellon University within the last 10 years for exceptional professional or vocational accomplishment.

One letter of support is required for all nominees, and up to two letters of support can be included. These letters are instrumental in the selection process for providing a complete account of the nominee's accomplishments, contributions and impact.

Nominations are accepted year-round and will be considered based on annual application deadlines.

Nominations remain active for two award selection cycles. If your candidate is not selected, you will have the opportunity to add supplemental and/or updated information to the individual’s nomination packet prior to the next deadline.

Awards are not presented posthumously.

Selected honorees must be present at the CMU Alumni Awards ceremony in order to receive an award.

Eligibility is limited by award type to alumni of Carnegie Mellon University.

Spring Carnival

Homecoming Weekend

Each fall, the CMU community puts on their best Tartan for a weekend of family-friendly activities like the annual CMU Alumni Awards, campus tours, Buggy previews and the tailgate and football game.

The Fence. All-night study sessions. Spring Carnival. Homecoming on a crisp fall day. Those traditions are part of your Carnegie Mellon University experience — and this space is your connection to those memories, whether you graduated 50 years ago or just last spring.

Please reach out if you need additional information or assistance — the CMU Alumni Association is here to help you stay connected to the university’s past, present and future. And check back frequently — exciting events and news are always on the way.

Angie Callen engineers high-potential careers

Jul 23, 2026

Angie Callen engineers high-potential careers

By Elizabeth Speed

“I’m a recovering engineer who loves people. That one sentence alone should tell you I was destined for the Sunday Scaries the minute I enrolled in Civil Engineering at Carnegie Mellon.”
These first two lines of Angie Callen’s book, "Scary Good: Discovering Life Beyond the Sunday Scaries," are an effective summary of why Angie and her new book are resonating with people who are wondering about their career directions.
The “Sunday Scaries” are Angie’s term for the workweek dread that often sets in when vocation and motivation don’t align. That’s where she found herself in 2003 as a freshly-minted graduate from Carnegie Mellon University. She was working as a civil engineer focused on physical infrastructure. Unfulfilled and isolated, she eventually realized the most important project she needed to rebuild was her own career.
Engineer or leader?
A problem solver at heart, Angie enjoyed the rigor of her undergraduate engineering training and its focus on process and analytical skills.

Angie Callen engineers high-potential careers

Engineer or leader?
A problem solver at heart, Angie enjoyed the rigor of her undergraduate engineering training and its focus on process and analytical skills. Doubts, such as her dislike of a first-year physics class, didn’t set off big alarms.
Angie’s energy was well-utilized as a campus leader. She was selected as a Head Orientation Counselor for new student orientation and was active in Greek life and the civil engineering department. Sporting a tasseled hard hat rather than a traditional cap at graduation in 2003, she brushed off lingering misgivings and remained optimistic about her path as an engineer.

Angie moved to Boston and began building her career in engineering, where she leaned into what was comfortable: leadership and connection. Her drive to build relationships created early-career opportunities that pushed her up the ladder quickly. In short order, she moved from a place on the team to leading it, which was a tall order for an engineer with under five years of experience.
“I was the poster child for grin and bear it,” she says.

“I was the poster child for grin and bear it,” she says. “But control and perfectionism were coping mechanisms. I was burning myself out attempting to maintain someone else’s version of success.”
In 2008, Angie was given the opportunity to transfer from Boston to Colorado, but rather than a dream assignment, the move turned into a wake-up call.
“For someone who thrives on impact and connection, showing up to a sterile cubicle to design paved parking on National Forest land so ski resorts could pack in more cars was soul-crushing,” she says.
Fortunately, a curveball in the form of the Great Recession helped her make big changes.
Economic downturn, career turnaround

Angie’s career salvation came in step with the economic downturn that began shortly after her move across the country. Construction projects halted, and furloughs and free time followed. Angie spent that time outside, met her husband Jim, and embraced a new passion: ski slopes, mountains and rustic trails as nature — not engineers — intended. That challenged her values and beliefs.

That challenged her values and beliefs. When she found joy outside, and outside of engineering, inevitably, she left engineering altogether.
What followed over the next few years was a revitalizing vagabond existence in both life and work. Her career change journey included jobs at an art gallery, an arts nonprofit, and a failing business. But by living lean, prioritizing time outside and connections with people, Angie began to find glimmers of gratification. Despite facing both bankruptcy and near homelessness in 2017, Angie persisted.
“What I learned is what real resilience is. It’s absorbing the hit,” Angie says. “I grieved what was gone, then started again with the pieces I could salvage, even feeling they were flawed and incomplete. It wasn’t about recreating the past but about building something new that would hold the weight of who I had become.”
The next phase of building was both literal and figurative. To solve their housing needs, Angie and her husband renovated a 30-year-old school bus and called it home full-time for four years.

She also realized her multiple career reinventions and life iterations were the elite training necessary to start a coaching business. She funneled that experience into the creation of Career Benders and The Modern Coach, career and leadership coaching firms focused on helping others with the same “Sunday Scary” feelings of being stuck, uninspired and in need of a new direction.
Bold and empowered
Though coaching may seem like a divergence from Angie’s start in engineering, in many ways it’s a full-circle return to where she started.
“I engineer human potential instead of buildings,” Angie says. “I started my career working in infrastructure, data and math-heavy systems, and now I get to work on the most complex, unpredictable, fascinating system of them all — people.”
Angie’s skills as a coach caught on, with dozens of her clients raving about her help in transforming their work to align with values and purpose.

Angie’s skills as a coach caught on, with dozens of her clients raving about her help in transforming their work to align with values and purpose. Over time, she’s continued to build her brand and expand her work in the leadership and career coaching spaces. She launched the “No More Mondays” podcast in 2021, a show to inspire others to live up to their full potential. Her book “Scary Good” was published in early 2026, garnering excellent reviews and three independent book awards. In the book, she shares her coaching philosophy framed by her personal journey.
Yet another transformation is in the works, as well. As a people-person in a tech world, Angie sees a tear in the cultural fabric forming with the onset of AI. People are increasingly isolated, and the same void-of-purpose that drives the Sunday Scaries is also rewiring traditional approaches to executive leadership and team-based work. Through speaking and consulting avenues, Angie is focused on improving communications, restoring connections and refocusing workplaces on the humans within them.

For more information, visit
AngieCallen.com

“What I learned is what real resilience is. It’s absorbing the hit. I grieved what was gone, then started again with the pieces I could salvage, even feeling they were flawed and incomplete. It wasn’t about recreating the past but about building something new that would hold the weight of who I had become.”
– Angie Callen (ENG 2003)

The HUB

Comprehensive & Integrated Enrollment Management

The HUB is Carnegie Mellon University’s one-stop-shop offering comprehensive services and counsel to enrolled students and families for
financial aid

billing and payments
,
registration activities
, and
academic records
. With the goal of supporting student enrollment and persistence, The HUB provides individualized attention and technologically responsive tools in a professional, welcoming and accessible environment.

About - The HUB - Division of Enrollment Management - Carnegie Mellon University

Find Your Liaison

Student Services Specialists

Student Services Specialists (SSS's) are The HUB's front-line response team. You can find them at the front desk greeting students, family members and other visitors, as well as answering phones, responding to emails and producing ID Cards. The SSS's have broad knowledge in all aspects of enrollment management and excellent customer service skills.
In 2023, the SSS's answered 12,958 questions from students

and 3,605 questions from parents
.

Meet The HUB Staff

Testimonials

"You supported and advocated for him each year and worked with us diligently finding ways to keep him in school. We will always remember your kindness."

~ Family of a CMU Alumnus

"You were so calm, patient, and professional. Also, you gave us advice and direction on how to proceed with finishing (our student's) finances."

~ Family of a CMU Undergraduate Student

"You've literally been the most supportive person I have had the pleasure of dealing with in college and if I could submit a review or survey or recommendation, I would give you a bazillion/10."

~ CMU Undergraduate Student

Plan Course Schedule

The University Registrar's Office collects course offerings from our academic departments to create the Schedule of Classes (SOC) each semester. Students may use the Plan Course Schedule feature in
Student Information Online (SIO)
to plan future schedules once the SOC is published. Students can also use
Stellic Degree Audit
to plan their schedules and track their progress toward earning their degree.

Related Info & Links:

Course Registration

Course Adds, Drops, Withdrawals & Voucher Elections

Grade Options: Pass/No Pass & Audit

Planning Your Schedule

Step 1: Browse the SOC

Published before each semester begins, the
SOC
displays the courses available in any given semester, listing courses, titles, meeting times, classroom assignments and instructor information. The SOC will also display course planning information such as course reservations and pre-requisites or co-requisites.

SOC for the CMU Community

SOC for the Public

Step 2: Check Your Progress with Stellic

Stellic Degree Audit Application
is a student-driven, collaborative academic planning tool that employs the university’s undergraduate catalog and degree requirements to assist students with schedule planning and staying on-track to graduate. Once registration week begins, you will register for courses within SIO. Information about registration start times and a step-by-step guide to the registration process are available on the

webpage.

Mellon College of Science Awards and Honors

Recognizing Students and Faculty for Research, Innovation and Academic Excellence
At Carnegie Mellon University, faculty and students from the Mellon College of Science are regularly honored — nationally and internationally — for their outstanding contributions to science, research and innovation. MCS also celebrates excellence within its own community through faculty awards, student scholarships and staff commendations.

Faculty Research Honors

MCS faculty, from laureates to rising stars, are renowned for their thought leadership, student mentoring and ceaseless innovation. Their achievements not only underscore their scientific advances but also how well they foster a cutting-edge learning environment for our students and researchers.

Student Awards and Honors

retrieval_text:
Carnegie Mellon’s Richard King Mellon Hall of Sciences Enters New Phase of Construction

With topping off completed, the Hall of Sciences’ “bones” are in place and interior and exterior finishing of the around 340,000-square-foot facility will begin.
When completed in 2027, the Richard King Mellon Hall of Sciences will be a place where science, technology, art and creativity converge at CMU in new and exciting ways. Extending CMU’s campus westward, the facility will house researchers and educators from the Mellon College of Science, School of Computer Science and the Institute for Contemporary Art (ICA) Pittsburgh, fostering a collaborative atmosphere that enables partnerships across disciplines. It will also create a new iconic gateway to campus, connecting CMU more closely to its Oakland neighbors, and include an expanded location for the ICA Pittsburgh that will elevate its role as a hub of art, culture and exchange.
Launched with a lead gift from the Richard King Mellon Foundation, the Hall of Sciences is designed with flexibility in mind, providing endlessly configurable spaces that can be mobilized quickly to answer emerging problems and respond to new avenues of discovery.
