“Open Stacks: Eyes on the Skies” Photo Gallery

by Sarah Bender
On Wednesday, Oct. 7, the
Posner Center for Special Collections
hosted its first Open Stacks event of the year. “Eyes on the Skies” celebrated humanity’s fascination with space, welcoming astronaut and Carnegie Mellon professor emeritus
Jay Apt
to give a talk titled “Spacewalking and What’s It Like Up There,” a firsthand look at living and working in space.
Apt outlined his journey to becoming an astronaut in the 1980s, including parachute training and water tank training, then shared details and photos from his time in space. He talked about seeing typhoons, dust storms, volcanoes, and the aurora from orbit, the work he did with his crewmates, and more. The audience had a chance to ask questions toward the end of his talk, prompting Apt to share more about the photography equipment used by astronauts, and offer advice to students dreaming of going into space today.
Rare books from
Special Collections
that traced the enduring effort to make sense of space were also on view.

Bodies of Horror
,” the next Open Stacks event, will be held on Wednesday, Oct. 28 from 4:30–6:30 p.m. in the Posner Center. Attendees who arrived early took some time to examine the rare books on display before finding their seats.

School of Drama students Madelyn Streisfeld and Alabaster Richard brought a time capsule for guests to add their watercolor paintings.

Richard and Streisfeld work on watercolor paintings of their own.

retrieval_text:
A Crucible of Change

A Crucible of Change

New Archives Exhibition Traces Carnegie Tech’s Transformation During World War I

In 1917, the Carnegie Institute of Technology was only 12 years old, still establishing its identity as a technical school in Pittsburgh. America’s entry into World War I abruptly changed its trajectory. Within months, classrooms, laboratories, and even the landscape of campus were being adapted to support a national mobilization, testing the young institution’s ability to respond at extraordinary speed and scale.
The University Archives’ new exhibition “
A Crucible of Change: Carnegie Tech and World War I
” traces that transformation. Presented across Hunt Library and Baker Hall, the exhibition draws on letters, photographs, artifacts and other materials from the University Archives and partner collections to tell a story that extends across campus — much as the war itself did more than a century ago.
Together, the installations explore how the difficult period tested the adaptability, creativity and bravery of the university community.

It was the beginning of a much larger mobilization explored through the “Nation at War” and “The War Courses” sections of the exhibition in Baker Hall.

The Tooters, 1918. The American Expeditionary Force operated over 200 bands in France with approximately 7500 musicians in total. World War I Records Carnegie Mellon University Archives.

Campus Trenches, 1918. To prepare students and soldiers for the type of war they would face in France engineering students learned to construct trenches on campus which were then used for rifle training. World War I Records Carnegie Mellon University Archives.

Over the next year, Carnegie Tech developed 13 additional war courses, putting its technical expertise to work preparing soldiers for an increasingly mechanized conflict.

retrieval_text:
A Crucible of Change

Over the next year, Carnegie Tech developed 13 additional war courses, putting its technical expertise to work preparing soldiers for an increasingly mechanized conflict. Training encompassed radio and buzzer operation, automobile and airplane maintenance, radio engineering, blacksmithing, coppersmithing, mechanical drafting, truck driving and other specialties. Carnegie Tech also operated a bandmaster training program, preparing two 50-person military bands through an intensive eight-week course.
For students, those changes were impossible to separate from everyday campus life. Wooden barracks rose on The Cut to house 1,000 men. An airplane hangar was built in 30 days, workshops expanded nearly overnight, and an outdoor forge was constructed for blacksmith training. Students marched and drilled, practiced grenade throwing and dug trenches in nearby Schenley Park. The campus was simultaneously a school, construction site, and military training ground.
The war also transformed opportunities for women. As explored in the exhibition’s “Women in War” section, Margaret Morrison Carnegie School developed intensive courses in stenography for government offices, chemical analysis for steel plants, and occupational therapy for disabled soldiers.

Steel companies and laboratories recruited women chemists for wartime work, only for many of those opportunities to disappear when the war ended.

Red Cross Nurses, 1918. Nurses assigned to care for the soldiers on campus pose in front of Margaret Morrison Carnegie College―Carnegie Tech’s women’s college. World War I Records Carnegie Mellon University Archives.

Dedication of the Langley Aeronautical Laboratory, 1918. Langley Aeronautical Laboratory was built in just twenty-three working days to provide a space for soldiers to learn how to repair airplanes. The dedication featured remarks from local dignitaries, troops in formation, and planes driven across campus to be housed in the new building. The building was named for Samuel Langley, an aviation pioneer and the first director of the Allegheny Observatory. World War I Records Carnegie Mellon University Archives.

By fall 1918, of the 3,593 students on campus, only 486 were civilians, most of them women. The rest wore uniforms.
“It is hard to imagine today just how much life changed on campus for students in 1918,” said Corrin.

A Crucible of Change

The rest wore uniforms.
“It is hard to imagine today just how much life changed on campus for students in 1918,” said Corrin. “One day, you came to campus for a football game. The next day, you were in a different kind of uniform practicing how to use a bayonet and learning military tactics.”
Lasting Legacy
More than a century later, the material record of that transformation forms the foundation of “A Crucible of Change.”
Striking black-and-white photographs throughout the Hunt Library installation show a campus reshaped by the war. In display cases, uniform coats, signal flags, a gas mask, mess kit, and more give physical form to experiences documented in photographs and written records.
“The University Archives mostly collects two-dimensional objects, such as documents and photographs. We're very grateful to our partners at
Soldiers & Sailors Memorial Hall & Museum
, who let us borrow artifacts to bring the story to life,” said Corrin. “These objects, which Pennsylvania soldiers carried with them overseas, help us remember that history happened to real people.

“These objects, which Pennsylvania soldiers carried with them overseas, help us remember that history happened to real people. They help us put ourselves in the shoes of students at that time.”

World War I was the first widespread use of government propaganda. These colorful propaganda posters were plastered across buildings in cities and towns urging individuals to join the military, purchase Liberty Bonds, or conserve food. In addition to celebrating the American war effort they vilified and dehumanized “the Hun” a pejorative used by the British and Americans to describe German soldiers.
All posters courtesy of the Library of Congress and the National World War I Museum.

Together, those materials allow the exhibition to look beyond military training to the ways war reached nearly every part of life at Carnegie Tech and throughout Pittsburgh. “Pittsburgh at War” places the university within an industrial city producing war material on an enormous scale, while “Civil Liberties and Protest” examines the disappearance of organized opposition to the war from campus as federal restrictions tightened and military participation became embedded in university life.

Another section explores how music, theater, art and writing became outlets for responding to the conflict. Carnegie Tech trained military bands, and members of the drama program contributed through performance and wartime pageants. English faculty member Haniel Long collected letters and poetry written by Carnegie Tech men in service, publishing them in “The Soldier’s Progress and Carnegie Tech War Verse” in 1918.
The surviving record also documents the human cost of that transformation. While the record is incomplete, approximately 900 Carnegie Tech students, alumni and faculty are known to have served during World War I. At least 44 students died in service.
History Across Campus and Beyond
The end of the war did not end its presence on campus.
Seven men’s residence halls — Henderson, Boss, McGill, Miller, Engelbrecht, Scobell and Welch — were named for Carnegie Tech students and alumni who lost their lives during the war. Plaques at the buildings commemorate those students; now, updated versions will add historical context about the people behind the names and their connections to Carnegie Tech.

A Crucible of Change

“Every space offers a different way into a story,” said Associate Director of Creative and exhibition designer
Heidi Wiren Kébé
. “When we bring exhibitions into the places where people study, work, and gather, we create opportunities for unexpected encounters with the Archives. Through thoughtful design, we can make those histories feel immediate and intimate. We help people see themselves as part of a larger, evolving story.”
The exhibition now extends beyond campus as well. Material from “A Crucible of Change” is on view at the
Pennsylvania Governor’s Residence
in Harrisburg, the official home of the governor since 1968 and a public space that uses art, historic objects, and educational programming to connect visitors with the Commonwealth’s history and culture.
“Taking this work beyond campus allows us to connect Carnegie Mellon’s history with broader Pennsylvania history,” said Kébé. “At the Governor’s Residence, Carnegie Mellon becomes part of a broader conversation about Pennsylvania and the people who shaped it.

Chasz Griego is a STEM Librarian at the Carnegie Mellon University Libraries, where he supports researchers, educators, and students in Chemistry, Chemical Engineering, and Materials Science and Engineering. He holds a Bachelor of Science degree in Chemical Engineering from the New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology (Socorro, NM), and a PhD in Chemical Engineering from the University of Pittsburgh. For his dissertation, he studied computational models that facilitate screening catalyst materials with quantum chemistry simulations. Chasz also leads and supports Open Science teaching and research initiatives at CMU, particularly in the areas of reproducibility in computational research. He regularly teaches and supports open source programming with Python for research.

G. Sayeed Choudhury is the Associate Dean for Digital Infrastructure and Director of the Open Source Programs Office (OSPO) at Carnegie Mellon Libraries and an affiliated faculty member of the Block Center for Technology and Society and Scott Institute for Energy Innovation, as well as the Executive Director of the Open Forum for AI.
He was the Director of a Alfred P. Sloan Foundation grant for coordination of University OSPOs and was a Co-Investigator for the Black Beyond Data Project. Choudhury is a member of the Open Source Initiative (OSI) Board, Human AI Collective Advisory Board - BGV & EAIGG, and Schmidt Sciences Humanities and AI Virtual Institute (HAVI) Advisory Board. He was the Software Area Expert and member of the Steering Committee for the Research Data Alliance (RDA) - US.
Choudhury was a President Obama appointee to the National Museum and Library Services Board.

retrieval_text:
Sayeed Choudhury

Choudhury was a member of the ECAR Data Curation Working Group. He has been a Senior Presidential Fellow with the Council on Library and Information Resources, a Lecturer in the Department of Computer Science at Johns Hopkins and a Research Fellow at the Graduate School of Library and Information Science at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. He is the recipient of the 2012 OCLC/LITA Kilgour Award.
Choudhury has served as principal investigator for projects funded through the National Science Foundation, Institute of Museum and Library Services, Library of Congress' NDIIPP, Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, Andrew W. Mellon Foundation, Open Society Foundation, Microsoft Research, and a Maryland based venture capital group.
Choudhury has published articles in journals such as the International Journal of Digital Curation, D-Lib, the Journal of Digital Information, First Monday, and Library Trends and presented at various open-source events hosted by the United Nations, Open Forum Europe, Open Ireland Network, and the Linux Foundation.

Alumni & Visitors

Alumni & Visitors

The University Libraries welcomes alumni and visitors to explore our spaces, attend our events, and utilize select services. We are happy to answer any questions and appreciate your suggestions for expanding our services.

Browsing & Borrowing

All visitors and CMU alumni are welcome to browse and use physical collections of books, bound journals, newspapers, and microfilm while visiting any of our library locations.

Please see staff at the Hunt Library Circulation desk to purchase a Special Borrower's card.

View
borrowing allocations
.

Use Library Spaces & Technology

The Libraries are open and accessible to all, regardless of affiliation with CMU.

As a visitor or CMU alum, you have two-hour access to computers in library locations with a guest pass. To get a guest pass, present valid photo ID at a circulation desk. The guest pass will automatically expire 24 hours from issuance.

Access Electronic Databases

Visitors and CMU alums have access to electronic databases while on campus in a library location. To access databases, obtain a guest pass as described above.
